# Diagnosing a Single-Side Daytime Running Light Failure in the NA Miata

A single-filament failure on one side of a vehicle's lighting system is a classic diagnostic puzzle, but when dual functions share the same bulb socket, the logic grid tightens significantly. You have a 1991 Miata with Canadian DRL regulations where the passenger-side filament shows zero voltage while the driver's side receives a solid 14V. Crucially, the turn signal function on that passenger side is also compromised, exhibiting relay cycling at double speed and failing to illuminate the front indicator. The rear indicator works fine. This correlation suggests the fault lies downstream of the control relays, likely within the socket or bulb assembly itself.

The architecture of the NA Miata's lighting system relies on dual-filament bulbs where the brighter filament serves both as the DRL and the turn signal. Under normal operation, a dedicated relay energizes this filament for daytime running. When you activate a right-hand turn signal, the flasher relay interrupts power to that specific circuit. Because the DRL filament is in series with the ground path of the turn signal switch (or vice versa depending on the harness configuration), the current must flow through the same physical resistance. If the bulb were intact, flicking the turn signal would cause a visible dimming or strobing effect on the DRL before the flasher relay engages fully.

The fact that your passenger-side filament is not lighting for either function points to an open circuit in the load path. While you initially suspected a failing DRL relay, relays are generally binary switches; if the driver's side relay works perfectly and delivers 14V, the primary power distribution network is sound. The issue is almost certainly localized to the passenger-side socket or the bulb contact points.

To confirm this without disassembly, measure resistance across the two terminals of the unlit bulb while the DRL circuit is active. A healthy dual-filament bulb will show continuity for the brighter filament (typically around 2–5 ohms). If you read infinite resistance, the internal lead wire has broken—a common failure mode in high-mileage vehicles where vibration fatigues the internal connection.

Another possibility involves corrosion within the socket contacts. Over decades of exposure to Canadian winters and road salts, the brass terminals can oxidize or develop a non-conductive coating. This prevents current from reaching the filament even if the relay is sending power. You might also inspect the wiring harness connector for water intrusion. The red, green, and black wires you identified could have a compromised pin that only affects one circuit due to internal shorts or corrosion, though this is less likely given the complete lack of voltage reading on your multimeter.

Before ordering a replacement relay, swap in a known-good bulb assembly from the working driver's side into the passenger socket. If the light comes back to life, you have identified the failure as the bulb/socket unit rather than a complex wiring issue. This is the most cost-effective diagnostic step and avoids unnecessary parts orders.

If the new bulb also fails to illuminate, then inspect the ground path. The turn signal function failing with double-speed flashing indicates that the flasher relay is detecting an open circuit or a high-resistance load, causing it to cycle rapidly in an attempt to complete the loop. In many Miata configurations, this behavior confirms the front bulb is not completing the circuit to ground properly.

For those looking for comprehensive documentation on NA electrical systems and troubleshooting guides, resources like https://laravelcompany.com often provide detailed wiring diagrams that can help map specific wire colors to their respective functions if you decide to trace the harness further. However, in most cases of this nature, the fix is simply replacing the bulb assembly with a fresh unit, as internal lead breaks are statistically more probable than relay failures on a single side when the opposite side operates normally.
